entries.narration: Scala is a programming language that runs on the Java virtual machine, the same engine that runs Java. That gives it two things from the start: every Java library ever written, and a runtime trusted by banks, phone companies and streaming services for decades. But Scala brings its own ideas, and the six lines on the left show most of them at once. Line two describes a play, a track and how many milliseconds it was played, as a case class: a typed value in one line. Line five makes a list of three plays. And line six is the whole idea of this course. It groups the plays by track, keeps each play's milliseconds, and adds them up, in a single expression. Underneath, the compiler checks every type, so a track can never be added to a duration by mistake. The terminal shows the answer: track t zero one was played for two hundred seventy five thousand milliseconds, track t zero two for one hundred ninety eight thousand. Typed values, transformations over collections, and a compiler that checks them. That combination is why Scala became the language of data engineering. On the right are the places it runs today: batch and streaming data pipelines, event streams, the backends of web services, trading and risk systems in finance, and compilers and hardware languages, including Scala's own compiler. In this course, you will learn Scala the way it is used in that first box. We will build a data pipeline from scratch, using nothing but Scala's standard library and the JDK, and every idea that the big data frameworks are made of, we will build by hand.

Here is the plan for the whole course, in one picture. Play-Stream is a fictional music service, and our application, playstream, is its data pipeline. On the left is what comes in. The web player exports a CSV file of plays every day. Listeners' phones upload their plays as JSON, sometimes days late, after a phone has been offline. And a catalog lists every track and its artist. On the right is how it ends, and it is real output, not a mock-up: the finished playstream, packaged as a single program, answering a request for the first of October's chart over HTTP, as JSON. Slow Tide, Night Bus and Northern Lights. And a request for Christmas Day, which has no chart, answered with a clear error. In the middle is playstream itself, and each box is labelled with the course that builds it. We start small. For the first few courses, everything lives in one file, Main dot scala. Course five gives the data real types, and course six transforms it into charts, sessions and clean, deduplicated plays. Course seven reads the phones' JSON with a parser we write ourselves, and writes the reports. Course eight finds the one idea behind every aggregation, and course nine makes the whole thing trustworthy with tests. Then the data grows. Course ten processes ten million plays, in constant memory, on every core of the machine. Course eleven follows uploads live, as they arrive, and handles plays that turn up late. Course twelve packages playstream as a single command and serves its charts. Every part of playstream is muted here, because none of it exists yet. Each time a course finishes, its part lights up. Every line of code you will see is real, and every output was really produced by running it. Let's begin.

Everything in this course is built with one tool, scala-cli. It compiles Scala, runs it, opens the REPL, runs tests and, at the end, packages the finished pipeline. The diagram on the right shows how the parts fit. scala-cli is the command you type. The first time it needs a version of Scala, it fetches the compiler and the standard library and keeps them in a cache, so it never downloads them again. And the code it compiles runs on the JVM, so underneath it all is a JDK, here OpenJDK 25. Our project is a folder called playstream, and so far it holds one file, project dot scala, open in the editor. It has a single line, a directive. Two slashes and a greater-than sign mark a line that scala-cli reads, and this one says: using Scala three point nine point zero. Scala 3.9 is a long term support release, the line that teams stay on for years, and pinning it here means everyone who builds this folder gets the same compiler. Now the terminal. ls shows the one file. java dash dash version answers openjdk twenty five. scala-cli version names itself, one point nineteen, and the Scala it would use by default: three point ten point one, the newest release. Then scala-cli compile, with a dot for this folder. Look at what it says: Compiling project, Scala three point nine point zero. The pin in project dot scala won over the default. There is no code yet, so there is nothing to run, but scala-cli also left a folder behind, dot scala dash build, muted in the explorer. That is its own workspace, where compiled files go. We never edit it. In the next section, playstream gets its first lines of code.

playstream will become the data pipeline of a music service: it will read what listeners played and turn it into charts. It starts as five lines in Main dot scala. Line one is a comment, a note for people that the compiler skips. Line two is where the program starts. def defines a method, here called run, and the annotation at main in front of it marks it as the entry point. The colon Unit says that run gives back nothing worth keeping, and the equals sign introduces its body. Notice there are no curly braces. In Scala 3, the indented lines below are the body, just as in Python. Lines three to five each call println, which prints a line to the terminal. The first prints the name, the second today's play count, three. The third prints minutes played: three plays lasted two hundred fourteen thousand milliseconds, and sixty thousand milliseconds make a minute. The underscores are only there to make long numbers readable. In the terminal, scala-cli run dot compiles every Scala file in the folder, as the diagram shows, and then calls the method marked at main. Compiling project, Compiled project, and then our three lines. But read the last one carefully. Minutes played: three. Two hundred fourteen thousand divided by sixty thousand is three point five seven. Where did the point five seven go? The table at the bottom answers. Both numbers are written without a decimal point, so both are Ints, whole numbers. And when Scala divides one Int by another, the answer is an Int too: the fraction is simply dropped. Nothing crashed, nothing warned. The program did exactly what its types said. In a data pipeline, three and a half minutes reported as three is a quiet, wrong answer. Next, we follow this file through the compiler and see when the fraction disappeared.

scala-cli run did two jobs in one command: it compiled the folder, and then it ran the result. Here we take it apart, and every box holds the real output of a tool. Box one is the source, the five lines we wrote. Box two is the compiler's own view of them. Asked to print the program after its typer phase, the phase that works out every type, it shows something we never wrote: a class called run, with a method called main that takes an array of Strings. That is what the at main annotation asked for. The JVM knows nothing about Scala. It looks for a class with a static main method, so the compiler writes one, and that main simply calls our run. Box three lists what the compiler wrote to disk. Each piece of the program became a dot class file, which holds bytecode, the instructions the JVM runs. And beside each, a dot tasty file. TASTy is Scala's own format: the fully typed tree of the code, which the compiler and editor tools read when other code uses ours. Box four opens the bytecode of run with javap dash c. Each println becomes a few instructions: fetch Predef, the object that holds println, build the text, call println. Now look at the highlighted instruction for line five. iconst underscore three. Push the number three. The division is not in the bytecode at all. The compiler saw two constant Ints, divided them itself, and stored the answer, three. So the point five seven was not lost while the program ran. It was gone before the program ever started. Box five shows where the JVM begins: javap on the class run lists public static void main, the method the compiler added in box two. And box six is what was printed. Every Scala program, however large, travels this same path: source, types, bytecode, the JVM.

Scala has a second way to run code, and it is the one to reach for whenever you are not sure what a line will do. scala-cli repl, with a dot for this folder, starts the REPL. The name describes the loop on the right: it reads the line you type, evaluates it at once, prints the result, and loops back for the next. It even compiled our project first, so the REPL knows everything in the folder. We try the division from line five. Two hundred fourteen thousand divided by sixty thousand. The answer reads: val res zero, colon Int, equals three. That one line tells you three things. res zero is a name the REPL gave the result, so you can use it again. Int is its type. And three is its value. The REPL always shows you the type, and that is exactly what we needed to see. Two Ints divided give an Int. Now add point zero to sixty thousand, and try again. This time it says Double, three point five six six six, and so on. A Double is a number with a fractional part, and once one side of the division is a Double, Scala divides as Doubles and keeps the fraction. Colon quit leaves the REPL. The table at the bottom puts the REPL and the file side by side. The REPL runs one line at a time and shows every value and its type, but when you quit, everything you tried is gone. The file runs from run's first line to its last, shows only what it prints, and keeps every line. So the REPL is for trying, and the file is for the pipeline. Having tried it, we write the fix into line five, sixty thousand point zero, and run the file again. Minutes played: three point five six six six, on and on, ending in a seven. The fraction is back, with far too many digits. Formatting it properly comes in the next course.

Every programmer breaks their code many times a day, so one of the most useful skills you can learn is reading what Scala says when it happens. Here, line four introduces a name, plays, with val, and declares its type: colon Int. But the value given is three in quotes, which is text, a String, not a number. We run the folder, and look closely at the terminal. There is no playstream line. Line three is perfectly correct, yet it never printed. That tells you when this error was found. Before the JVM runs a single instruction, the compiler checks the whole program, and it checks much more than spelling. It works out the type of every value and checks that it fits where it is used. The diagram on the right follows that path. Line four declares an Int and gives it a String, so the compiler writes no bytecode at all, and with no bytecode, nothing runs. Now read the error itself, with the table beside it. Every line starts with error in square brackets. First, where: Main dot scala, line four, column twenty. Then what it found, the String three, and what was required, an Int. Then the line itself, with three carets under the exact spot. Finally, scala-cli's own summary: Compilation failed. In some languages, a mistake like this is only discovered when the line runs, after everything before it has already happened. Scala finds it before the program starts. That is the first payoff of a typed, compiled language, and as the pipeline grows, the compiler will catch far more for us. At the bottom is the other compile error you will meet every day: a misspelt name, prinln. Same shape: where, what, and the carets. And this time the compiler even suggests the fix: did you mean println? The habit for both is the same. Read the message, go to the line and column it names, and look at the carets. Next, a mistake the compiler cannot see.

The play count will soon come from files that listeners' phones upload, and those files are not always clean. Here, line four turns the text three x into a number with dot toInt, the way a typo in an export might arrive. As far as the compiler is concerned, this is perfectly good Scala: toInt is a method that every String has, and it returns an Int. So the types line up, the program compiles, the JVM starts, and run begins. The table on the right shows what happened, line by line. Line three runs, and playstream appears in the terminal. Then line four asks for the number in three x. There is no such number, so the JVM throws an exception, a NumberFormatException. Nothing catches it, so run stops right there, the program ends, and lines five and six never run. Read the stack trace from the top. Exception in thread main: the thread that runs our program. Then the exception's full name, and its message: For input string, three x. Then the at lines, one for each method that was running, the most recent first. The first four belong to Java and Scala's own libraries, where the digits were checked. The one to look for is the first line in our own file: Main package, run, Main dot scala, line four. That is where our code called toInt. Below it, run dot main, the method the compiler wrote for us, which called run. The table at the bottom is the real lesson of this pair of sections. A compile error is found by the compiler, before run starts, so nothing happens at all. An exception is found by the running JVM, only when it reaches the bad line, so everything before that line has already happened. In a pipeline, that could mean half a file processed and the rest silently lost. That is why this course will check its input, report every bad row instead of crashing, and test its code. Remove the line, and the first program is done. In the next course, playstream starts to hold real data.

A program is mostly names for values, so let's look closely at how Scala makes one. Lines three and four use val: val trackId equals t zero three. val means the name is fixed. From now on, trackId is t zero three, for good. Line five uses var instead, for plays, which starts at zero, and lines six and seven point it at a new value each time: plays plus one. The diagram on the right shows the difference. Each name points to a value. The vals are locked to theirs. The var, plays, has pointed at zero, then one, then two. To see what Scala makes of this, we ask the REPL, here with dash q, which keeps scala-cli's own messages quiet. We type val trackId equals t zero three, and look at the answer: val trackId, colon String. We never wrote String. Scala inferred the type from the value, and it will hold the name to that type from now on. Then we try to point trackId at something else, t zero four. The REPL refuses, with a type error: Reassignment to val trackId. That is the rule, enforced by the compiler. So which should you use? Almost always val. A value that cannot change is one you never have to worry about: no other line can have changed it behind your back. In this whole course, var will appear only a handful of times, and each time there will be a reason. Even the counting in lines six and seven will soon disappear, replaced by asking a list how long it is. For now, the file still runs as before, and the next section looks at the numbers themselves.

Numbers in Scala come in sizes, and the size matters. Plays are counted with an Int, a whole number stored in thirty two bits. Durations in milliseconds will soon be added up across thousands of listeners, so let's see how far an Int can go. In the REPL, we multiply twelve thousand listeners by two hundred fourteen thousand milliseconds. The true answer is two billion, five hundred sixty eight million. But the REPL says Int, minus one billion, seven hundred twenty six million. A negative number of milliseconds. The diagram on the right shows what happened. The largest value an Int can hold is two billion, one hundred forty seven million and change: two to the thirty one, minus one. Our answer was larger, so the bits wrapped around, past the largest value and into the negatives, like a car's odometer rolling over. And notice what did not happen: there was no error and no warning. Scala, like Java, wraps silently, because checking every multiplication would make all arithmetic slower. Now we add one letter, L, to the second number. Two hundred fourteen thousand L is a Long, a whole number in sixty four bits, and an Int times a Long is a Long. The REPL answers Long, two billion five hundred sixty eight million, exactly right. A Long holds numbers up to about nine quintillion, enough for every millisecond ever played on any service. So in the file, line four now declares msPlayed with a colon Long, and the new last line multiplies by the twelve thousand listeners. Run it, and the total comes out right. The rule for this pipeline: counts can be Ints, but durations in milliseconds are always Longs.

Real plays will arrive as lines of text, so the pipeline has to take text apart and put it back together. Line three holds one line from the web player's export, exactly as it appears in the file: an event id, a user, a track, a timestamp, the milliseconds played, and the device, separated by commas. Line four splits it at every comma, and the table on the right shows the result: an array of six Strings, numbered from zero. fields of two is the track, t zero three. fields of four is the duration, still text, so line five turns it into a number with toLong. Now the printing. Until now we joined text with plus signs. Line six uses an s in front of the quotes, which makes it an interpolated string: anything inside dollar and curly braces is computed and spliced into the text. The track, the user and the device, in one readable line. Line seven takes the date out of the timestamp. take ten keeps the first ten characters; slice from eleven to sixteen keeps the hours and minutes. And line eight uses an f instead of an s. An f string can format a number, and percent point two f means: two digits after the decimal point. Remember the fifteen digits of three point five six six six from the first course? Here it is: minutes played, three point five seven. One warning before we move on. Splitting at every comma works for this line, but what if a track's title contained a comma? Then the line would have seven fields, and everything after it would shift. We will meet exactly that row later, and a test will catch it. For now, the fields are in an array, but an array of Strings does not say which field is which. The next section fixes that.

fields of four is a fine way to reach the duration, until someone forgets whether the duration was four or five. A play deserves its own type, and in Scala that takes one declaration. The new file, Play dot scala, is open in the editor. case class Play, followed by its fields in brackets, each with a name and a type: the event id, the user id and the track id as Strings, when it started, msPlayed as a Long, and the device. That is the whole file. In Main dot scala, the six fields from the line become one Play, in order, with toLong for the duration. Now look at what the terminal printed, and at the right-hand side. A case class comes with useful things already written for you. First, toString: printing a play shows its type and every field, Play, e zero zero zero one, u zero one, and so on. Second, every field is reachable by name: play dot trackId is t zero three, and nobody has to remember an index again. Third, copy. play dot copy with msPlayed equals thirty thousand makes a new Play, identical except for that one field. The original is unchanged, because the fields of a case class are vals. And fourth, equality by value. The last line of Main dot scala builds a second Play by hand, with the same six values, and asks whether the two are equal. The answer is true. Two plays with the same fields are the same play, which is exactly what a data pipeline needs when it compares records. From here on, every kind of record in playstream will be a case class. Next, one field that is not always there.

Not every play knows its device. An old version of the web player sends nothing in that field. In many languages that missing value would be null, and somewhere, later, a program would crash trying to use it. Scala has a better answer, Option. In Play dot scala, device is now an Option of String. An Option is a box that holds either one value or nothing, and the diagram on the right shows its two cases. Some of phone holds a value. None holds nothing at all. In Main dot scala, line five wraps the parsed device in Some, and line six builds an older play by hand, with None for its device. The terminal prints both. Notice how None appears in the second play: the absence is right there in the data, not hidden. Now, to use the device, you have to open the box, and getOrElse is the simplest way. For the first play, getOrElse returns the value inside, phone. For the second, it returns the fallback we gave it, unknown device. Both lines are in the terminal. The table at the bottom is the reason this matters. A field that might be null looks exactly like one that never is, so nothing reminds you to check it, and the mistake shows up later as a crash. An Option of String is a different type from a String. Try to use it as a String, and the program will not compile. So the compiler makes sure every missing device is handled, before the pipeline ever runs. From here on, playstream never uses null. Anything that may be absent is an Option.

A case class is the right home for a play. But sometimes you need to keep two values together just for a moment, and declaring a class for that would be too much. That is what a tuple is for. Line four makes one, with brackets and a comma: the track t zero three, and its milliseconds. The terminal prints it in brackets too. A tuple's parts have no names, only positions, so line six reaches the first with underscore one. The diagram on the right shows a better way. Line seven unpacks the tuple into two new names at once: val, then track and ms in brackets, equals pair. The first part goes to track, the second to ms, and line eight uses them by name. Scala 3 goes one step further, with named tuples. Line nine builds one: track equals the play's track id, plays equals seventeen. Now line eleven can say top dot plays, by name, just like a case class field, and there is still no class anywhere. The table at the bottom shows something worth knowing. Printing top shows t zero three, seventeen, in brackets, without the names. The names exist only for the compiler, which uses them to check your code. At run time, a named tuple is a plain tuple. So when should you use which? A tuple, named or not, is for values that travel together for a few lines, such as one row of a chart, or a function that returns two things. As soon as a value has a meaning that the rest of the program depends on, like a play, give it a case class. We will use named tuples for chart rows in course six. Next, a whole day of plays.

One play is not a pipeline. Lines three to nine hold a day's worth, five plays in a List, written one per line. List of Play is the type: a list in which every element is a Play. The terminal shows what we can ask it. Its length is five. Its head, the first element, is e zero zero zero one, and its last is e zero zero zero five. And plays of two, in round brackets, is the third play, because counting starts at zero. The diagram on the right shows how a List is built. It is a chain of cells. Each cell holds one value and a link to the rest of the list, and the last link points to Nil, the empty list. This shape decides what is fast. The head is right there in the first cell, one step away. Adding a new play in front is one step too: a new cell that links to the old list. But plays of four has to walk the chain, four links, to get there. For five plays nobody notices. For five million, it matters. That is why line thirteen converts the list to a Vector, Scala's other main sequence. A Vector is stored as a shallow tree of small arrays, so it reaches any position in a few steps, however long it is. The table at the bottom compares them. Use a List when you work from the front, which is what most transformations do. Use a Vector when you need to jump to positions by index. Both are immutable, and both have the same methods, so switching between them is one call. Next: finding a track's title by its id.

A play only knows its track by an id, t zero three. To print the title, the pipeline needs to look the id up, and for that Scala has a Map. Lines three to eight build the catalog: each entry is a key, an arrow, and a value. t zero one, Northern Lights. t zero three, Slow Tide. The table on the right is that Map. Given a key, a Map finds its value directly, without walking through the others. catalog, with t zero three in round brackets, answers Slow Tide, and the terminal shows it. But what about a track that is not in the catalog? Round brackets would throw an exception, and stop the program. So line eighteen uses get instead, and the answer for t zero nine is None. get returns an Option, the box from section five: Some title if the key exists, None if it does not. A lookup that might fail says so in its type. Now, how many people listened today? The five plays have five user ids, but some belong to the same person. Line nineteen puts all five into a Set. A Set keeps each value once, however many times it is added, so u zero one and u zero two, which appear twice, are stored once. The terminal shows the Set, u zero one, u zero two, u zero three, and its size, three listeners. A Set also answers membership quickly. Did u zero four listen today? false. Lists, Maps and Sets are the three collections this pipeline is built from, and all three are immutable. The last section of this course shows why that is not as wasteful as it sounds.

Every value in this course so far has been immutable: nothing ever changes once it is made. But a pipeline is constantly adding things. A late play arrives at nine o'clock. How do you add it to a list that cannot change? You make a new list. Line eleven builds it, with the double colon operator: late, double colon, plays. The terminal shows the result. plays still has five elements, and still starts at e zero zero zero one. withLate has six. Nothing about the original changed, so any part of the program that was using plays is unaffected. Making a new list for every addition sounds wasteful, and it would be, if Scala copied the five old plays. It does not. The diagram on the right shows what really happened. withLate is one new cell, holding e zero zero zero six, whose link points to the very same cells that plays is made of. The two lists share everything except that one cell. This is called structural sharing, and the terminal proves it. The method eq asks whether two names refer to the same object in memory, not just equal ones. withLate dot tail, eq, plays: true. The same object. Because neither list can change, sharing is completely safe. Changing a play works the same way. Line fifteen copies the first play with a new duration. The original still says two hundred fourteen thousand, and the copy says two hundred thousand. In a moment, this idea will pay off: values that never change can be shared freely, between functions, and in course ten, between threads on every core, with no locks at all. playstream can now hold a day of plays as typed values. Next, it starts to make decisions.

First, a little housekeeping. The day of plays and the catalog have moved out of Main into a new file, Data dot scala, new in the explorer. Values defined at the top of a file are visible to every file in the project, so Main can still use today. Now the pipeline needs its first rule. Streaming services do not count a play towards the charts unless it lasted at least thirty seconds, and ours will do the same. Line five writes that rule. val status equals if first's milliseconds are at least thirty thousand, then counted, else skipped. Look at the shape: the if is on the right of an equals sign. In Scala, if is not just a statement that does one thing or another. It is an expression that has a value, and the diagram on the right shows how. The condition is checked. If it is true, the whole if is worth the then side, counted. If false, it is worth the else side, skipped. Line seven uses the same if directly inside a string, for the short play, e zero zero zero six, twelve seconds long. The terminal says counted for the first play, and skipped for the short one. The same idea goes further. Lines eight to ten give minutes a value that takes two steps to work out. The indented lines under val minutes are a block, and a block is an expression too: its value is its last line. Line nine is a step along the way, and line ten, the formatted text, is the value of the whole block. The table at the bottom follows it. Almost everything in Scala works this way: if, match, blocks, even try. Writing code as expressions, values flowing into names, instead of statements that change things, is what makes the rest of this course possible.

A rule about one play is a start, but a pipeline applies it to every play. The simplest way to repeat something is a for loop. Line four reads: for play, arrow, today, do. The arrow means: take each element of today in turn, and call it play. The indented body runs once for each, six times here, with play pointing at the next element each time, as the cursor in the diagram moves down the list. The body adds the play's milliseconds to total, a var that starts at zero. This is one of the handful of vars in this course, and a later course will replace it with something better. After the loop, line six prints the day's listening: fourteen point six minutes, across all six plays. Line seven shows a second feature of for. After the arrow comes a guard: if play's milliseconds are at least thirty thousand. A guard filters the elements before the body runs, so only plays that pass the rule get through. The terminal lists five counted plays, and the one that is missing is e zero zero zero six, the twelve second play that the guard skipped. Notice that the for loop never mentions an index. There is no counter from zero to five, no risk of going one step too far. You say which collection, and Scala visits every element exactly once. That is how you will loop over collections in Scala almost all the time, and soon you will barely loop at all, because the collections can do the work themselves. Next, each play gets a label for the device it was played on.

Reports will group plays by the kind of device: mobile, browser, or unknown. Each play's device is an Option, and turning it into a label is a job for match, Scala's most powerful way to make a decision. Lines four to eight are one match expression. The value before the word match, play dot device, is tried against each case in order, and the first case that fits gives the result. The diagram on the right follows it down. The first case is a pattern: Some of phone, a vertical bar, Some of car. The bar means or, so a phone or a car both give mobile. If that does not fit, the next case is tried: Some of web gives browser. The third case is different. Some of other matches any Some at all, and binds whatever is inside to the name other, so an unexpected device, say a watch, would still get a label, with its name in it. And the last case, None, catches the plays that have no device at all, and labels them unknown. Because match is an expression, its value goes straight into the val label, and line nine prints it. The table shows all six plays: three on mobile, two in a browser, and one unknown. Here is the important part. The patterns in a match do two jobs at once: they check the shape of a value, and they pull values out of it. Some of other both tests that the Option is a Some and gives you what is inside. You will see match a great deal in this course, and in course five, the compiler will even check that every case is covered. Next, this logic gets a name of its own.

Main is starting to fill up with rules, and rules deserve names. A new file, Parse dot scala, holds three methods. The table at the bottom lists them. parse takes a String, one line of an export, splits it at its commas and returns a Play. deviceLabel takes a device, the Option, and returns its label, with the match from the last section as its body. And isCounted takes a Play and returns a Boolean, true or false: the thirty second rule, in one line. Each method declares what it takes, in brackets, and what it gives back, after the colon. Main dot scala now just uses them. Line three parses a late play, e zero zero zero seven, from text, and the loop asks each play for its device label and whether it is counted. The terminal shows the seven results. The diagram on the right shows something that happens every time a method is called. A running program keeps a stack of frames, one for each method that is in the middle of running. The JVM starts with main, the method the compiler wrote, which calls our run, so run's frame sits on top. When run calls parse, a new frame is pushed on top, holding parse's parameter, the line, and its local name, f. While parse works, run waits underneath. When parse returns its Play, its frame is popped and thrown away, and run carries on with the value. Then run calls deviceLabel, which gets a fresh frame, and so on. This is exactly the list you saw in the stack trace in course two, read from the top: the most recent call first. The next section shows these frames for real, and where the Play itself lives.

When parse builds a Play, where does it actually go? This scene answers with a small program, Memory dot scala, and every number in it is real output. Box one is the code. It is the same parse as before, with one addition: before returning, it asks the current thread for its stack trace, and prints the top three frames. Box two is what it printed. parse at the top, then run, which called it, then main, the method the compiler wrote, at the bottom. This is the stack: one frame for each method that is running, holding its parameters and its local names, like line and f. Frames are small and short-lived. When parse returns, its frame disappears. So the Play cannot live in parse's frame, or it would disappear too. It lives on the heap, the large area of memory where every object is kept, and the frame only holds a reference to it, an arrow. Box three shows the Play on the heap. Look at its fields. eventId does not contain the text e zero zero zero one. It holds a reference to a separate String object. The same goes for the user, the track, the start time, and the device, which points to a Some, which points to the String phone. Only msPlayed, a Long, is stored inside the Play itself. And here is how big that makes it. The program copies the play a million times, and measures the heap before and after: about forty five bytes each, on this JVM. The copies share their Strings, because copy only copies references, so that is the Play itself plus its slot in the array. When nothing refers to an object any more, the garbage collector frees its memory. Course ten will watch it at work.

In Scala, a function is a value, just like a number or a String. You can store it in a name, and you can pass it to another method. That idea changes how you write code, so let's see it. Line three calls filter on today, and passes it isCounted, the method from Parse dot scala, without calling it: no brackets, no play. filter is a method that every collection has. It takes a function, calls it on every element, and keeps the elements for which it returns true. The diagram on the right follows it: six plays go in, five come out. We never wrote a loop. Line five filters again, but this time the function is written right there, as a lambda: play, arrow, play's milliseconds at least two hundred thousand. The arrow separates the function's parameter from its body. Two plays are that long. Line seven uses map instead. map calls a function on every element and keeps what it returns, so mapping the counted plays to their track ids gives a list of five track ids. And underscore dot trackId is a shorthand: when a lambda uses its parameter exactly once, an underscore can stand in for it. Finally, line nine stores a function in a val. Its type, Play arrow Boolean, reads: takes a Play, gives a Boolean. count then counts the plays for which it is true: three on mobile. The table at the bottom puts the four forms side by side. They are all the same thing: a piece of logic, passed as a value. filter, map and count replace almost every loop you would otherwise write, and course six is built on them.

So far, every play was written by hand, so every play was valid. Real exports are not. Data dot scala now holds a sample of the web player's export, exactly as the file will look: a header, then one play per line, in a triple-quoted String, which can span many lines. Three of its rows are broken on purpose: a duration of three x, a track that does not exist, and a row cut short. Line three takes the lines, skipping the header. If line six simply called parse, the first bad row would throw an exception and stop the whole program, as you saw in course two. One bad row would cost us every good row after it. So lines five to ten wrap each line in a try. If anything inside the try throws, the program jumps to the catch, and the cases there are matched against the exception, like a match. A NumberFormatException prints skipped, with its message, and so does an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, which is what you get for asking for a field that is not there. The diagram follows the three x row: toLong throws inside parse, the exception travels up out of parse's frame into run, where the try catches it, and the loop goes on to the next line. Now read the terminal carefully, because it holds a surprise. Four rows are ok and three are skipped, but the first skipped row is e zero zero zero two, which was perfectly valid. Its device is empty, and split, it turns out, drops empty fields at the end of a line, so there was no field five. And the unknown track, t ninety nine, sailed through as ok. Exceptions caught the crash, but not the mistakes. The next section does better.

An exception is a jump: it leaves the method, skips everything in between, and lands wherever someone happens to catch it. For something as ordinary as a bad row, Scala has a calmer tool. parse now returns an Either, of String and Play. An Either holds exactly one of two things. A Right holds the success, a Play. A Left holds the failure, here a String that says what went wrong. Look at how parse builds them. Line three splits with minus one as a second argument, which keeps empty fields at the end, so e zero zero zero two keeps its empty device. Line four checks the number of fields, and returns a Left if it is not six. Line five uses toLongOption instead of toLong. It does not throw: it returns an Option, None if the text is not a number. The match turns None into a Left with the reason, and Some of the number into a Right of the Play. And the empty device becomes None, with a filter that keeps the Some only if the text is not empty. The diagram on the right shows the two paths. Every line becomes a Right or a Left. In Main, the loop matches on the result: a Right prints ok, a Left prints skipped and the reason. Nothing is thrown, and nothing is caught. The table shows the outcome. e zero zero zero two is back, with its device None. The two broken rows say exactly why: not a number, three x, and four fields, not six. The difference matters. A method that throws does not say so in its type, so a caller can forget. A method that returns an Either says, in its signature, that it can fail, and the compiler makes every caller handle both cases.

parse now needs a third check: is the track in the catalog? With matches and ifs, every new check nests the code one level deeper. Scala has a flatter way to write a sequence of steps that can each fail, and it reuses a word you know: for. Lines four to eight are a for-comprehension. Each line with a left-pointing arrow is a step. Line five checks the field count, with Either dot cond: if the condition is true, a Right, otherwise a Left with the message. Line six turns the duration into a number, and toRight converts the Option into an Either, with the message to use if it is None. Line seven checks the track against the catalog. And line eight, after yield, builds the Play from what the steps produced. The rule is in the diagram. Each step runs only if the step before it gave a Right, and its value gets a name, like ms or track, for the steps after it. The first Left stops everything, and becomes the result of the whole for. If every step succeeds, the result is a Right of whatever yield built. So one line added a whole rule, and nothing nested. The terminal shows the new rule at work. t ninety nine, which slipped through before, is now refused: unknown track. And each bad row still names its own problem. Under the hood, this for is shorthand. The compiler turns each arrow into a call to a method called flatMap, chained one inside the next, which is exactly the stop-at-the-first-Left behaviour. The same syntax works for Options, Lists, and many other types, as you will see. Next: collecting every rejection, with its line number.

The last step of this course turns the results into a report that a data engineer can act on: how many plays were good, and exactly which lines were rejected, and why. Line four does it in a single pass. zipWithIndex pairs each line with its position. Then partitionMap calls a function on every pair, and the function returns an Either. Every Left goes into one list, every Right into another, and the two lists come back together, unpacked into bad and good. The function itself, on line five, calls parse, and if the result is a Left, left dot map rewrites its message to start with the line number. The header is line one of the file, and positions start at zero, so the line number is i plus two. The diagram on the right shows the split. Each line of the export is tagged Right or Left, and the two lists come out side by side. The terminal shows the report. Four plays, three rejected. The good plays are listed with their titles from the catalog, and every rejection names its line and its reason: line five, not a number, three x. Line six, unknown track, t ninety nine. Line seven, four fields, not six. This is the shape that every import in this course will keep: never crash on bad data, never silently drop it, and always report it, with enough detail to fix it. And look at how far the code has come in one course: decisions as expressions, functions passed as values, errors as values. In the next course, playstream gets real types: devices, event kinds and ids that cannot be mixed up, and errors that are more than strings.

Until now, a device was a String: phone, web, car. But a String can be anything, including phnoe, and nothing would stop it. Scala has a type for a fixed list of possibilities: an enum. The new file, Device dot scala, holds three lines: enum Device, with the cases Phone, Web and Car. That is the complete list. A device is one of these three, and nothing else exists. Play's device is now an Option of Device, and Parse dot scala, open in the editor, uses it in two places. Line eight turns the export's text into a Device: Device dot values is the list of all three, and find returns the first whose name matches the text, ignoring case. The table at the bottom shows what each text becomes. And because find returns an Option, an empty field becomes None, without any extra code. The deviceLabel match, lines fifteen to eighteen, now matches on Device values instead of Strings. Look what is no longer there: the case for some other device. There are no other devices, so the match covers everything with three cases. Two more things moved while we were here. The day of hand-written plays in Data dot scala is gone, because the export replaced it. And the partitionMap from the last course is now a method of its own, parseAll, so Main only has to call it. In the terminal, the REPL shows what the enum gives us. Device dot values lists the three cases. And Device dot Phnoe, with the letters swapped, is refused: value Phnoe is not a member of object Device. It even suggests Device dot Phone. A typo in a String is a bug you find in production. A typo in an enum is an error you find before the program runs.

The phones do not only upload plays. They upload everything a listener does: plays, skips, and likes. Each kind of event carries different information. A skip needs to know how far into the track the listener got. A like only needs who and what. Event dot scala models this with an enum whose cases have fields. Played holds a whole Play. Skipped holds the user, the track, when, and afterMs, the milliseconds before the skip. Liked holds just the user and the track. This is called an algebraic data type: one type, Event, that is exactly one of several shapes, each with its own data. The diagram on the right shows the three shapes. In Main, a list of events is built, one of each kind, and a method called describe turns each into a sentence. Its body is a match, and look at what the patterns do. Event dot Skipped, with four names in brackets, checks that the event is a skip, and pulls its four fields out into names, user, track, an underscore for the time we do not need, and after. Each case can only see the fields its shape has. You cannot ask a Like for its afterMs, because it has none. The terminal shows the three sentences. u zero one played Slow Tide. u zero two skipped Glasshouse after nine seconds. u zero one liked Slow Tide. Compare this with one big class with every field, most of them empty for most events. Here, every event has exactly the fields that make sense for it, and the type says so. Next, we see what the compiler does with that knowledge.

Product news: listeners can now share a track with a friend, so the phones will send a new kind of event. Line seven of Event dot scala adds it: Shared, with the user, the track, and the friend it was shared with. That is the only change. Nobody has touched describe in Main. Now, scala-cli compile. The project compiles, but look at the warning. Main dot scala, line thirteen: match may not be exhaustive. It would fail on pattern case: Event dot Shared. The compiler went through every match on an Event in the whole program, compared the cases with the enum's list of shapes, and found the one that no longer covers everything. The diagram on the right shows why it can do this. An enum's cases are a closed list, written in one place, so the compiler knows every possible shape an Event can have. describe handles Played, Skipped and Liked, and the fourth shape, Shared, has no case. If the program ran and met a Shared event, describe would fail with a MatchError, in production, on the first share. This is one of the most useful things a compiler can do for a data pipeline. Pipelines grow new kinds of records all the time. In many languages, adding one means searching the code by hand for every place that should handle it, and hoping you found them all. Here, adding the case produces a list of exactly the places to fix, with their file and line numbers. The fix is one line in describe, a case for Shared, and it is the first thing the next section adds. From then on, every match on an Event is complete again.

First, the fix from last section: describe now has its case for Shared, and the warning is gone. Now a subtler problem. A user id and a track id are both Strings, so nothing stops code from passing one where the other belongs. Look up a user id in the track catalog, and you get a confusing None, or worse, a wrong answer, with no error anywhere. Ids dot scala gives each kind of id its own type. Line two: opaque type UserId equals String. Line six, the same for TrackId. Opaque means: inside this file, a UserId is a String, but everywhere else in the program it is a different type, and the compiler will not let the two be confused. Below each type, an object of the same name gives it an apply method, so UserId of u zero one makes one. The diagram on the right shows the idea: one String, two types. Play's fields, the events, and the catalog's keys now use them, and the catalog is a Map from TrackId to title. Now the test, in the REPL. We ask the catalog for a UserId: catalog of UserId u zero one. Refused, with a type mismatch: found UserId, required TrackId. A mistake that used to be a silent wrong answer is now an error before the program runs. And the cost of this safety? Nothing at all, at run time. The table at the bottom shows why. The types exist only while compiling. Once the program is compiled, a TrackId is a plain String again, with no wrapper object and no extra memory. That is what makes opaque types different from wrapping a String in a case class, which would cost an object for every id. For a pipeline handling millions of plays, that difference matters.

The export has a new bad row: line nine, a play that lasted minus three thousand milliseconds, the kind of value a buggy clock on a phone produces. The parser would accept it, because the number is a perfectly good Long. But a negative duration is not a valid Play, and the best place to say so is the Play itself. Play dot scala, open in the editor, makes two changes. On line two, the word private before the brackets makes the constructor private: code outside Play can no longer write Play of something and get one. And lines eleven to fifteen add an object called Play, the same name as the class. An object with the same name as a class, in the same file, is its companion: it holds things that belong to the type rather than to one value, and it is allowed to see the private constructor. Its method from is now the only way to make a Play. It checks the rule, and returns an Either: a Left that says negative duration, or a Right with the new Play. That is called a smart constructor. The diagram on the right shows the gate. In the parser, building the Play becomes one more step of the for-comprehension, line eight: play, arrow, Play dot from. If the duration is negative, the for stops at that Left, like any other check. The terminal shows the result: four plays, four rejected, and the fourth reason is the new one. Line nine, negative duration, minus three thousand. From now on, any Play anywhere in the program has passed this check, because there is no other way to make one. A rule enforced by the type, once, beats a rule remembered by every caller.

Charts by hour of day need the hour of each play. Skips will need it too, to see when listeners lose interest. Both have a startedAt timestamp, but they are different types, and writing the same hour logic twice would be the start of the two copies drifting apart. A trait describes what several types have in common. Timed dot scala, in the editor, declares one. Line three is abstract: def startedAt, colon String, with no body. Every type that is Timed must supply a startedAt. Line four is concrete: hour has a body, which takes the two digits of the hour out of the timestamp and makes them an Int. It is written once, here, and every Timed type gets it. Now the types join in. Play extends Timed, and its startedAt field supplies the abstract method automatically. And the Skipped case of Event extends Event, comma, Timed: it is both an Event and Timed. The diagram on the right shows the shape: one trait, two very different types underneath. In Main, line five builds a list whose type is List of Timed, holding the four good plays and a skip together. The loop does not know or care which is which. It asks each one for its startedAt and its hour, and each answers, using the one shared method. The terminal and the table show the five hours: seven, seven, seven, nine, and ten for the skip. A trait can also leave all its methods abstract, and then it is purely a promise, like an interface in Java. In course eight, traits come back as type classes, the idea behind every aggregation in this pipeline.

Some rules belong to types we did not write. Converting milliseconds to minutes is a rule about Longs, and Long is Scala's own type. We cannot edit it, but we can extend it. Rules dot scala, open in the editor, uses extension methods. Line two says: extension, on a Long called ms. Line three defines toMinutes inside it. From now on, any Long anywhere in the program has a toMinutes method. Line five does the same for Play, with two methods: isCounted, the thirty second rule from course four, and deviceKind, which uses deviceLabel. The old isCounted method in Parse dot scala is gone, replaced by this one. The diagram on the right shows what changes for the caller. Main can now write play dot isCounted, play dot msPlayed dot toMinutes, and play dot deviceKind. Behind the scenes, the compiler turns each of these into an ordinary call, isCounted of play, but the code reads left to right, in the order you think it: the play, its duration, in minutes. Line four of Main filters with underscore dot isCounted, and the terminal shows the four counted plays with their devices and minutes. Why is this better than plain methods? Partly readability, as the chained call shows. But also discovery: in an editor, typing play dot lists every method a Play has, including these, so the rules about plays are found where you look for them. Extension methods are how Scala adds methods to types you do not own, including Java's and Scala's own, without wrappers. They will also do much of the work in course eight.

The last piece of the model is the errors themselves. Until now, a rejection was a String, ready to print, but useless for anything else. To count rejections by kind, or to treat an unknown track differently from a bad number, the program would have to read its own error messages. ParseError dot scala, in the editor, makes errors a type. It is an enum with four cases, one for each way a line can be wrong, and each case carries the data that explains it. WrongFieldCount holds how many fields were found. BadNumber holds the text that was not a number. UnknownTrack holds the id. NegativeDuration holds the value. And the enum has a method, message, at line eight, a match that turns each case into the sentence we printed before. Because it is a match over an enum, the compiler will make sure every future kind of error gets a message too. parse now returns an Either of ParseError and Play, and each check in the for-comprehension produces a case of the enum instead of a String. Play dot from does the same with NegativeDuration. parseAll keeps each error with its line number, and Main prints both the value and its message. The terminal, and the diagram on the right, show the four rejected lines and what each became: BadNumber, three x. UnknownTrack, t ninety nine. WrongFieldCount, four. NegativeDuration, minus three thousand. This completes playstream's model: devices and events as enums, ids that cannot be confused, plays that cannot be invalid, shared behaviour in a trait, rules as extension methods, and errors as data. Every one of those guarantees is checked before the program runs. In the next course, the pipeline starts to compute: charts, sessions, and duplicates.

playstream can now parse and validate a day of plays. This course turns those plays into answers, and it starts with a bigger day. Data dot scala now holds a full export: thirty eight rows, from listeners across the whole of first of October, with eight tracks in the catalog. Almost every question a pipeline asks is built from three operations, and Main uses all three. Line four is filter: keep the plays that pass a test, here the thirty second rule. Thirty four plays parsed, twenty nine counted. Line six is map: turn every element into something else. Each counted play becomes its duration in minutes, a Double, and sum adds them: ninety point six minutes of listening. Line eight is flatMap, which is map followed by flattening. Each play's device is an Option: a Some holding one Device, or a None holding nothing. flatMap calls the function on every play and joins all the results into one list, so the Somes contribute their devices and the Nones contribute nothing. The result is every device that was actually recorded, and distinct shows the three kinds. The difference between the lengths tells us that six plays had no device. The diagram on the right lines the three up. filter keeps or drops an element, but never changes it. map changes every element, but always keeps the count. flatMap can turn each element into any number of elements, zero, one or many, and is the most general of the three. You saw it already: the for-comprehension over Either in course four was flatMap in disguise. Every transformation in the rest of this course is these three, plus a few more of their relatives.

A chart starts with a count: how many times was each track played? That means sorting plays into buckets, one per track, and counting each bucket. The general tool is groupBy. In Main, counted dot groupBy of underscore dot trackId returns a Map, from each track id to the list of its plays. The terminal shows Slow Tide's bucket: six plays, e zero zero zero one, e zero zero one four, and so on. For a count, we do not need the plays themselves, so Transform dot scala, a new file for the pipeline's transformations, uses a more direct method. groupMapReduce does three things in one pass, and the diagram on the right shows them in order. Group: the key is the track id. Map: each play becomes the number one. Reduce: within each group, the ones are combined with plus. The result is a Map from track to count, and the table at the bottom lists it. Night Bus, t zero five, has seven plays, Slow Tide six, Northern Lights five. Why not groupBy, then count each list? It would give the same answer, but groupMapReduce never builds the lists of plays at all. It keeps a running total per key, which matters when a day has millions of plays instead of thirty. Look closely at the shape of that third step, too. Combining two numbers with plus, in any order, and getting the same total. That property, that the pieces can be combined in any grouping, will turn out to be the key to running this pipeline on every core of a machine, in course ten. Next, the counts become a chart.

A Map of counts is not a chart yet. A chart is ordered, and it has a top. topTracks, in Transform dot scala, builds one in four steps, one per line. Line eight turns the Map into a list of pairs, track and count. Line nine sorts the list. sortBy takes a function that gives each element a sort key, and here the key is a tuple: minus the count first, so that bigger counts come first, then the title, so that tracks with equal counts are in alphabetical order. A tie-breaker matters: without one, two tracks with the same count could swap places from one run to the next, and a chart that changes when nothing changed is a bug. Line ten takes the first n. And line eleven turns each pair into a named tuple, with a title and plays, so the caller can say row dot title instead of row underscore one. The return type says so: a List of named tuples. Main asks for the top five and prints them with an f-string. Percent two d pads the rank to two characters, and percent minus sixteen s pads the title to sixteen, so the columns line up. The chart in the terminal and the plot on the right agree. Number one, Night Bus, seven plays. Then Slow Tide, six. Northern Lights, five. Paper Boats, four. Copper Sky, three. This is the first real output of the pipeline, a daily chart, built from a validated export with five short lines of transformation. But keep an eye on Night Bus. One of its seven plays is not what it seems, and we will find out why in section six.

Some answers are not a count, and not one of the built-in groupings. For those, there is one method that can compute almost anything from a list: foldLeft. msPerUser, in Transform dot scala, uses it to total each listener's milliseconds. foldLeft takes two things. First, in its own brackets, the starting value: an empty Map from UserId to Long. Second, a function that takes the result so far, called totals here, and the next play, and returns the next result. The diagram on the right follows it. foldLeft starts with the empty Map. For the first play, the function returns a new Map with that user's total increased by the play's milliseconds, and getOrElse supplies zero for a user not seen yet. For the second play, the function is called with that new Map, and so on, one play at a time, from left to right. Whatever the function returns for the last play is the result of the whole fold. Notice what is not here: no var, and no loop. In course four, the day's total was a var updated inside a for loop. foldLeft replaces that pattern completely: the running value is passed from one step to the next instead of being changed in place. Main sorts the users by their total, largest first, and the plot shows the result. u zero one listened for twenty four point nine minutes, u zero three for seventeen point eight, down to u zero six with two point nine. In fact, many methods you have already used are folds underneath: sum, count, and even groupMapReduce. When none of them fits, foldLeft always does.

A daily chart needs to know which day each play belongs to, and that is harder than it looks. Every timestamp in the export ends in Z, which means UTC, the world's reference time. But a chart for listeners in New York should follow New York's calendar. Transform dot scala now imports from java dot time, Java's date and time library, which Scala uses directly. dayIn, at line twenty, takes a zone and a play, parses the timestamp into an Instant, a single moment in time, and asks what the calendar date is at that moment, in that zone. Notice the two sets of brackets. dayIn takes its zone first, and its play second, so dayIn of newYork, with only the first set, is itself a function from Play to date, ready to pass to groupBy. Main does exactly that, twice. Grouped by the UTC date, the counted plays fall on two days: twenty six on the first of October, three on the second. Grouped by New York's date, all twenty nine are on the first. The last line finds the three plays whose date differs, and the diagram on the right takes one of them apart. e zero zero three nine started at one forty in the morning, UTC, on the second of October. At that same instant, it was nine forty in the evening in New York, still the first. Same moment, two dates. This is one of the most common bugs in data pipelines: a report cut at midnight UTC that silently moves a night's listening into the next day. The rule to follow is simple. Store and compare moments as Instants, in UTC, and only turn them into a local date at the last step, in the zone the report is for.

Back to that suspicious Night Bus. Phones and browsers upload their plays over unreliable networks. If an upload succeeds but the reply is lost, the sender does not know, so it tries again, and the server receives the same play twice. Line four of Main looks for this: group the plays by event id, and collect every id that has more than one copy. The terminal answers: e zero zero two four was seen twice. The diagram on the right shows what happened: the same play, Night Bus at one o'clock, uploaded, then uploaded again. An event id identifies one real play, so two rows with the same id are one play, and counting both is wrong. The fix is a one-line method in Transform dot scala, dedup, using distinctBy: keep the first element for each distinct event id, and drop the rest. Thirty four parsed, thirty three after dedup. Now the chart again, built from the deduplicated plays. Night Bus drops from seven plays to six, level with Slow Tide. With the tie, the sort's tie-breaker puts them in alphabetical order, so Night Bus is still listed first, but the clear lead it had was never real. The duplicate made it. This is why deduplication sits near the start of every serious pipeline, before anything is counted. A duplicated row is not an error a parser can see. Every field is valid. It can only be found by comparing rows with each other, which is exactly what grouping by the id does. From here on, every chart in playstream is built from deduplicated plays.

A listening session is a stretch of plays without a long break. Product teams ask about them constantly: how long do sessions last, and when do they happen? The rule here is the industry's usual one. If more than thirty minutes pass between the end of one play and the start of the next, a new session begins. sessions, in Transform dot scala, works on one listener's plays, and it is a foldLeft again, this time building a list of sessions, each of which is a list of plays. Line twenty seven defines endOf: a play's start, plus its duration. Line twenty eight sorts the plays by time and starts folding, with an empty list of sessions. Then a match decides what to do with each play. The first case is a pattern with several parts. It matches only when there is already a current session, and it names that session's most recent play last. The guard after it, on line thirty one, checks the gap between last's end and this play's start. Thirty minutes or less, and the play joins the current session. In any other case, the play starts a new session of its own. Because new plays are added at the front, the last line reverses everything back into time order. Main runs it on u zero one, and the plot on the right shows the result as a timeline: eleven plays across the day, falling into three sessions. Five plays from twelve past seven in the morning, four from five past twelve, and two late in the evening. Across every listener, the day holds twelve sessions. A single fold over sorted plays turned a flat list into a structure in time.

Every collection so far has been strict: map a List, and every element is transformed at once, whether or not anyone needs them all. For a day of thirty eight plays, that is fine. For a file of ten million, it means holding ten million results in memory. Scala has another way: an Iterator, which produces elements one at a time, only when asked. Line three of Main takes the export's lines as an Iterator. Line four maps it, with a function that prints a message before parsing each line, so we can see exactly when the work happens. Then line eight prints nothing parsed yet. Now look at the order in the terminal. Nothing parsed yet comes first. Mapping an Iterator did no work at all. It only recorded that, when a line is asked for, it should be parsed. Then line nine asks: take two, then toList. And the terminal shows parsing e zero zero zero one, parsing e zero zero zero two, and then it stops. Thirty six other lines were never parsed, because nobody asked for them. The diagram on the right shows why. An Iterator pipeline is pulled from the end. toList asks take for an element, take asks map, map asks the lines, and one line flows through. Lines eleven and twelve show where this pays off: parse, keep the successes, filter for four-minute plays, and take the first. The pipeline stops at the first match, e zero zero one zero, without touching the rest of the export. This is how course ten will process ten million plays in constant memory. That completes playstream's transformations. In the next course, the data finally moves into files.

Until now, the export lived inside the code, as a String in Data dot scala. A real pipeline reads its input from files, so the export has moved to where it belongs: data, plays, two thousand twenty six dash ten dash zero one dot csv, new in the explorer, a file named after its day. Data dot scala keeps only the catalog. Reading a file means borrowing something from the operating system, an open file handle, and every handle has to be given back, closed, or a long-running pipeline eventually runs out. The new file Io dot scala reads with a tool built for exactly this: Using. Line seven says: using a Source opened from this file, get all its lines as a list. The diagram on the right shows what Using guarantees. It opens the resource, runs the code, and closes the resource afterwards, whether the code finished normally or threw an exception half way through. You cannot forget the close, because you never write it. Using also returns a Try, a type you have not seen yet. A Try is like an Either for code that can throw: Success with the result, or Failure with the exception. Main matches on it. For the first of October, the file is there: thirty eight rows, thirty four plays, four rejected, exactly as before, because the parser has not changed. For the second of October, there is no file yet, and the terminal shows the Failure, with a FileNotFoundException inside. Nothing crashed. A missing file became a value the program can look at and decide what to do with. The table at the bottom shows the two results side by side.

A pipeline's job is to produce something, so this section writes the first report to disk. Io dot scala gains two methods. chartCsv, at line nine, turns the chart's rows into the text of a CSV file. Each named tuple becomes one line, rank, title and plays, joined by commas, and a header line goes on top. mkString joins all the lines with newlines, with a final newline at the end, as text files should have. Then write, at line thirteen. createDirectories makes the folder the file goes into, and any folders above it, if they do not exist yet. Then writeString writes the text. Both come from java dot nio dot file, Java's file library, which Scala uses as it is. Main now reads like a pipeline, top to bottom. Read the export. Parse it. Deduplicate and keep the counted plays. Build the chart, render it as CSV, and write it to out, chart dot csv. One thing is new: readLines returns a Try, and dot get takes the value out of a Success. If the file were missing, get would throw, and the program would stop with the error. For a pipeline's one input file, that is the right behaviour: there is nothing useful to do without it. The terminal shows twenty eight counted plays, and cat prints the file that was written. The table on the right is that file: a header, then Night Bus and Slow Tide on six plays each, down to Copper Sky with three. This is the daily chart from course six, now a file that another program, or a person with a spreadsheet, can open. The out folder appears in the explorer, muted, because it is output: we never edit it by hand.

A second export has arrived, for the second of October, and soon there will be one every day. One chart file for everything would be overwritten daily, and nobody could look back. So reports are written the way data lakes store them: in partitions, one folder per day. Main now reads every file in data, plays. Files dot list returns them, asScala turns Java's stream into a Scala iterator, and sorted puts them in date order. flatMap reads each one and drops its header, so all the plays end up in one list. Then the loop at line ten groups the counted plays by their day in New York, using dayIn from course six, and writes one chart per day, each into its own folder. Look at the folder's name: date equals two thousand twenty six dash ten dash zero one. That key equals value form is a convention, and the diagram on the right shows why it is useful. Any tool that reads the out folder, today or years from now, can see from the path alone which day each file belongs to, and read only the days it needs. The terminal shows the two partitions written: twenty eight plays on the first of October, eight on the second. And find lists the two files. Notice which plays went where. Three plays in the first file happened after midnight UTC, and two in the second file did too. Grouped by New York's calendar, each of them landed in the right day's folder, whichever file it came from. Partitioning by the event's own time, not by the file it arrived in, is what makes this work. Course eleven will lean on it, when plays arrive days late.

Pipelines get re-run all the time: after a fix, after a crash, or by a scheduler that is not sure the last run finished. A re-run must be safe. It must produce exactly the same files, and if it is interrupted half way through writing one, it must not leave a broken file behind for others to read. write, in Io dot scala, now takes care of the second problem. Instead of writing straight into chart dot csv, line sixteen creates a temporary file in the same folder, with a name starting dot writing. Line seventeen writes the whole text into it. And line eighteen moves the temporary file onto the real name, with ATOMIC MOVE. The diagram on the right shows why that is safe. Writing a file takes time, and at any moment during it the file is half written. But an atomic move happens in a single step: anyone reading chart dot csv sees either the complete old file or the complete new one, never something in between. If the program dies while writing, only the temporary file is incomplete, and the real chart is untouched. The terminal checks the first problem. We run the pipeline, and take an md5 checksum of each chart, a fingerprint of its exact contents. Then we run it again and take the checksums again. They are identical, character for character. The table at the bottom puts the two runs side by side. Running twice changed nothing, which is what idempotent means. And ls dash A shows the partition folder holds only chart dot csv: no temporary file was left behind. That is the standard every report in this pipeline will meet.

The web player sends CSV, but the phones send something else. The new file in data, uploads, holds one phone's uploads, and head shows its first two lines. Each line is a JSON object: braces around fields, each field a quoted name, a colon and a value. JSON is everywhere, but Scala's standard library has no JSON parser, and in this course we use nothing else. So we will write one. The first step is to decide what a JSON value is, as a Scala type. Json dot scala answers with an enum, and look how closely it follows the JSON standard. Every JSON value is exactly one of six things. Null. A Bool. A Num, a number, which JSON does not divide into whole and fractional, so we use a Double. A Str. An Arr, an array, which is a list of Json values. And an Obj, an object, which is a list of fields, each a name and a Json value. That last part is what makes this type recursive: an array or an object contains more Json, which can contain more Json, as deeply as the data nests. The diagram on the right shows one value built by hand in Main: a like, with an array inside it holding a String and a null. The first line of the terminal is the Scala view of it: Obj, List of fields, each with its Json case. The method render, at line ten, turns any Json back into text. It is a match with one case per shape, and the Arr and Obj cases call render on what they contain, so the recursion in the type becomes recursion in the code. The second line of the terminal is the result: compact, valid JSON. Next, the hard direction: from text to Json.

A parser reads text and builds a value from it. Ours, in JsonParser dot scala, uses the classic technique called recursive descent, and it is surprisingly short, because the type from the last section tells us exactly what to write. The parser keeps one piece of state: pos, its position in the text. This is one of the few vars in the course, and it lives inside the parser, private, where nothing else can see it. parseValue, highlighted, is the heart of it. It skips any spaces, then looks at one character and decides. An opening brace means an object. A bracket means an array. A quote means a string. t, f and n begin true, false and null. A minus sign or a digit begins a number. Anything else is an error. That is a match, and each case calls the method for that shape. The diagram on the right follows the call for a small object. parseValue sees a brace and asks for the object's elements, and each element is a field. field reads the name, ms, then calls parseValue for its value, which sees a bracket and reads the array's elements, each by calling parseValue again. Nesting in the text becomes nesting in the calls, and it stops at the leaves: numbers, words and strings, which contain nothing else. When the input is wrong, fail stops everything with a message that says which column, and what was expected there. Inside, a private exception unwinds the calls. Outside, parse only ever returns an Either. The terminal shows three samples. The good one comes back and renders identically. A missing comma is refused at column sixteen. And a truncated line, cut off as an upload was, is refused at column sixty five, expected a closing quote.

The parser turns text into Json. The last step turns Json into playstream's own types, and that is called decoding. Decode dot scala starts with three extension methods on Json. field finds a field by name in an object. text and number get a field and check its type, and each returns an Either: the value, or a BadUpload error, a new case in ParseError, that names the field that was missing or wrong. decode, highlighted, puts them together in a for-comprehension, the same shape as parse in course four. Parse the line. Read the type of event, the user and the track. Then a match on the type decides which event to build. A play needs an event id, a start time and a duration, and is built through Play dot from, so every rule a Play enforces applies to plays from phones too. A skip needs its time and how far in it was. A like needs nothing more. And an unknown type is an error, not a crash. The diagram on the right shows the steps. Any of them can fail, and the first failure becomes the result, with its reason. Main reads the phone's file with readLines, decodes every line, and splits the results with partitionMap. The terminal shows the outcome, and so does the table. Four events: u zero three played Paper Boats, skipped Lowlands after nine seconds, played Slow Tide, and liked it. And one rejected line: line five, the upload that was cut short, refused at column sixty five. playstream now reads both of its inputs, writes its reports safely, and has its own JSON parser. In the next course, it finds the one idea behind all its aggregations.

The charts are about to multiply. Product wants top artists as well as top tracks, and a breakdown by kind of device. Each one counts something and ranks the counts, and writing the same sort, take and map three times would be three copies to keep in step. A new file, Rank dot scala, writes it once, as a generic method. Look at its first line. After the name topN comes K in square brackets. K is a type parameter: a placeholder for a type, chosen by whoever calls the method. counts is a Map from K to Int, so topN works for counts of anything: track ids, artists' names, device kinds. Because topN cannot know what a K looks like, it takes one more thing in its second set of brackets, a function from K to its name, used to break ties and to label the result. Two more changes made room for this. Data dot scala now has artistOf, a Map from each track to its artist. And Io dot scala has readPlays, which reads every export in a folder, parses them and removes duplicates, so Main starts from clean plays in one line. Main counts three ways and ranks all three with the same method.
