The diagram on the right shows K taking three values: TrackId, with the catalog as its name function, and String twice, with identity, the function that returns its argument unchanged. The terminal shows the three top threes, now over both days. Slow Tide leads the tracks with ten plays, Mara Quell the artists with fourteen, and mobile the devices. The compiler checked every call: passing a name function for the wrong type of key would not compile. Generic code is written once and checked for every type it is used with.

Timed dot scala gains a small method, earliest, which takes a List of Timed things and returns the one with the earliest start. Main calls it with a List of Play. And with a list of plays and skips added together. Both work, and the terminal shows the earliest play, and the earliest of both, a skip at two minutes to seven. But should the first call work? earliest asks for a List of Timed, and plays is a List of Play. Those are different types. It works because every Play is Timed, and Scala's List is declared with a plus sign on its type parameter: List of plus A. That plus makes List covariant: if Play is a Timed, then a List of Play is a List of Timed. The diagram on the right shows the rule. It is safe for List because a List cannot change: nothing can sneak a skip into a list that is meant to hold only plays. Now the same code with an Array, in a branch of the spine. An Array can be changed in place. If an Array of Play could be passed as an Array of Timed, the method receiving it could store a skip into it, and the caller, still believing it holds only plays, would find a skip where a play should be. So Array is invariant, with no plus sign, and the compiler refuses. The side terminal shows the real error: found an Array of Play, required an Array of Timed. You will rarely write a plus sign yourself, but you will rely on it constantly. It is the reason immutable collections can be passed around so freely: a collection of a specific type can stand in for a collection of a more general one.

topN takes a function to name its keys, but for a sort it really needs something more basic: a way to order them. Scala has a type for that, Ordering, and Rank dot scala now asks for one. Look at the first line. topN's second set of brackets says using, Ordering of K. A using parameter is one the caller does not normally pass. Instead, the compiler finds a value of that type, a given, and passes it automatically. For String, Scala's library already has one. For our TrackId and UserId, which are opaque types, there is none: the compiler does not look inside an opaque type, even when it is a String underneath. So Ids dot scala adds one to each companion object: given, Ordering of TrackId, equals the String ordering. Inside Ids dot scala, where a TrackId is a String, that is allowed. The diagram on the right follows the search for topN of byTrack. The method needs an Ordering of TrackId. The compiler looks in the usual places, including the companion of TrackId itself, and finds our given. And then it does something more. sortBy sorts by a pair, minus the count and the key, and needs an Ordering for that pair. Nobody wrote one. The compiler built it, from the given for Int and the given for TrackId, because the library has a given that makes an Ordering for any pair whose parts have one. The terminal shows the result. Track ids sort correctly, t zero one to t zero eight. The ranked tracks and artists come out with no Ordering written at either call. givens are how Scala passes context, such as how to order, compare or combine a type, without anyone threading it by hand.

Look back at every aggregate this pipeline computes. A count adds ones. A total adds milliseconds. A Map of counts per track merges two Maps, adding the counts for the same track. They are all the same shape: a way to combine two values, and an empty value to start from. That shape has a name, Monoid, and Monoid dot scala captures it as a trait with a type parameter. A Monoid of A has empty, and combine, which takes two As and returns one. On its own, the trait does nothing. What makes it useful are its instances, as givens, one per type. Int's empty is zero and its combine is plus. Long's is the same. And the third given, at line seventeen, is the clever one. It says: for any Map from K to V, if V has a Monoid, then the Map has one too. Its empty is the empty Map, and combining two Maps keeps every key, combining the values for keys that appear in both, with V's own combine. This pattern, an interface implemented outside the types it describes, and found by the compiler as a given, is called a type class. Int knows nothing about Monoid, and never had to change. Line six adds an operator for it, an extension method called pipe plus pipe, available on any type that has a Monoid. The terminal and the table show it on four kinds of value: three plus four is seven, two Longs, two Maps of play counts, where t zero three's counts were added to make three, and the empty Map. One operator, three types, chosen by the compiler from the types alone. The diagram on the right shows the trait and its instances.

With a Monoid for each type, every aggregation in this course becomes the same three words. combineAll, at line twenty nine, folds a list of values, starting from the Monoid's empty and combining each value into the result. Written once, it works for anything with a Monoid. Main shows two uses. The first turns each counted play into a tiny Map, its track id to one, and combineAll merges them into the plays per track: t zero three ten, t zero five seven, t zero one six, the same as groupMapReduce gave. The second is where it gets interesting. Each play becomes a pair: one, and a Map from its user to its milliseconds. And the given at line twenty five says that a pair of two things with Monoids is itself a Monoid, combining each side separately. So one combineAll, in a single pass over the plays, computes two answers at once: thirty six plays in total, and the minutes for each of eight listeners. u zero one, twenty four point nine minutes, as foldLeft found in course six. The diagram on the right shows the pass. Here is why this matters, and why it was worth a whole course. Remember the property from course six: combining in any grouping gives the same answer. Add ones in pairs, or in fours, or split the plays into eight piles, total each pile and then total the totals: the result is the same. A Monoid's combine is required to have that property, called associativity. In course nine, a test will check it. And in course ten, it is exactly what lets the pipeline split ten million plays across every core, combine each part separately, and still get the right answer.

Every report so far was written by a hand-made function like chartCsv, which knew the exact columns of one row type. Adding a report meant writing another. CsvCodec dot scala replaces all of them with a type class whose instances the compiler writes for us. A CsvCodec of A knows two things: the header, a list of column names, and how to turn one A into a row of cells. Now look at the bottom of the file. case class ChartRow, with a rank, a title, an artist and plays, and then the words derives CsvCodec. That asks the compiler to create a given CsvCodec for ChartRow, by calling derived, at line ten. derived is inline, which means it runs at compile time, inside the compiler. It asks for a Mirror of the case class: the compiler's own description of it, including the names of its fields, as types. constValueTuple turns those names into values, a list of Strings. The diagram on the right shows the steps. And the rows come from productIterator, which every case class has: its fields, in order. toCsv, folded away between them, takes rows of any type with a CsvCodec and writes the file. Main builds the chart as ChartRows and the listeners as ListenerRows, and writes both. The terminal shows the two files. Each header was never typed anywhere: rank, title, artist, plays came from ChartRow's fields, and user, plays, minutes from ListenerRow's. Add a field to a case class, and its CSV gains a column, checked at compile time. Generic methods, givens, type classes and derivation: with these, playstream says each idea once. In the next course, we prove it works.

Every section so far ended with us reading the terminal and agreeing that the output looked right. That does not scale. A pipeline needs checks that run themselves and fail loudly, and that is what tests are. Two lines in project dot scala bring in the course's first dependencies, test only, so the pipeline itself still uses nothing but the standard library. The using test dot dep line adds munit, a small test framework, together with ScalaCheck, which we will meet in section three. The javaOpt line silences a warning that JDK twenty five prints about a method Scala's own library still uses. A new folder, test, holds the tests. scala-cli treats every file ending in dot test dot scala as a test, compiled separately from the pipeline. ParseTest is a class that extends munit's FunSuite, and each test inside it has a name and a body. The first, a good row becomes a Play, is drawn on the right. It runs the unit under test, parse, on one line of the export. Then assertEquals compares what it obtained with what we expect: the event id e zero zero zero one, and the device, Some of Phone. The second test checks that three x comes back as a BadNumber. In the terminal, scala-cli test, with dash v for verbose output after the two dashes, compiles the tests and runs them. Each test reports its name and a plus sign: both passed. The table at the bottom shows the result, two tests, none failed. If the parser ever changes so that either answer differs, this command fails, and munit prints the obtained value, the expected one, and the difference between them. From now on, this is how playstream proves it still works.

Course four collected one bad row for every kind of ParseError, and every one deserves a test. Writing four nearly identical tests would be four copies of the same code. Instead, the test file now holds the cases as data. badRows is a list of pairs, written with an arrow: a line of the export, and the error it must produce. Three x must be a BadNumber. t ninety nine, an UnknownTrack. The short row, a WrongFieldCount of four. And minus three thousand, a NegativeDuration. Then a for loop, inside the test class itself, registers one test per pair. Its name is built from the line's event id and the error's message, and its body checks that parse gives exactly that Left. The diagram on the right shows the fan-out: one table of cases, one named test for each. The terminal lists all five tests, the good row and the four refusals, each with its own name and its own plus sign. This matters when a test fails. A single test looping over four rows would fail as one, and you would have to dig out which row broke it. Four separate tests fail separately, and the name tells you exactly which row and which rule. It also makes the cases easy to grow. When the next bad row turns up in production, with a problem nobody thought of, the fix starts with one new line in badRows, a test that fails, and only then a change to the parser. The list doubles as documentation, too. Anyone reading it sees every way a line can be wrong, next to an example, in one place.

A test with an example checks one case that someone thought of. A property checks a rule, against hundreds of cases that nobody thought of. MonoidTest uses ScalaCheck, through munit's ScalaCheckSuite, to check the rule that course ten depends on: that combine is associative. Look at the first property. forAll takes a function of three Maps, a, b and c. ScalaCheck generates them itself: random Maps from Strings to Ints, empty ones, huge ones, negative counts, odd keys. For each triple, the function checks that combining a with b first, then c, gives exactly the same Map as combining b with c first, then a. By default, it tries a hundred triples. The diagram on the right shows the loop. The second property checks the other law of a Monoid: combining anything with empty, on either side, changes nothing. The table at the bottom states the two laws. In the terminal, run with test only MonoidTest so that only this suite runs, both properties pass. Two hundred random cases, and the rule held every time. That is much stronger evidence than a few examples, because the cases include the ones a person would not think to write: two Maps that share every key, or none, or a Map with one key mapped to zero. It is also the right kind of test for this code. The Monoid instances will soon be used in ways we cannot list in advance, on data we have not seen. What we can promise is the law, and a property tests the law directly. Next, a property that does not pass.

Here is a property that checks something that sounds obviously true. CsvTest says: write a chart row with any title, read the line back, and you get the same four cells. Gen dot asciiPrintableStr generates random titles made of printable characters, and the property writes each one with toCsv and reads it back with readCsvLine, a new method in CsvCodec dot scala, which splits the line at its commas. The fixed seed near the top makes ScalaCheck generate the same titles on every run, so a failure can be reproduced exactly. And it fails. The terminal is filtered with grep down to the three lines that matter. Falsified after thirty six passed tests: thirty six random titles worked, and the thirty seventh did not. Then the most useful line of all. ScalaCheck did not stop at the long, random title that failed. It shrank it, trying smaller and simpler titles, until it found the simplest one that still fails: a title that is just one comma. The diagram and the table on the right show why. Written out, a comma in the title becomes one more comma in the line. Read back, the line splits into five cells instead of four. This is exactly the warning from course three, when we first split a line at its commas. A real song can be called Hello, World, and a chart with that song in it would have been written as a corrupt CSV file, with every column after the title shifted by one. No example test caught it, because nobody wrote that example. The property found it in under a second, and handed us the smallest possible case. The fix comes first thing in the next section.

First, the fix. CsvCodec dot scala now quotes a cell that contains a comma or a quote, doubling any quotes inside it, the way the CSV standard says, and readCsvLine reads quoted cells back. The terminal shows CsvTest passing again, with the same seed: the comma title and every other title now survive the round trip. Now, logging. Until now the pipeline reported what it did with println, which mixes messages for the operator with the program's real output, and has no notion of how serious a message is. The JDK has its own logging, with no library needed, and Log dot scala wraps it in two lines. log is the logger for playstream. info logs at level INFO, for normal progress, and warn at level WARNING, for things someone should look at. readPlays, in Io dot scala, now logs as it works: how many files and plays it read, a warning for every rejected line, with its line number and reason, and how many duplicates it dropped. Main logs the report it wrote. The diagram on the right shows where a message goes: the logger hands it to a handler, which formats it and writes it to standard error, kept apart from the program's own output. The format comes from a javaProp line in project dot scala: the level, the logger's name, and the message. The table at the bottom shows this run's log. Two files read, forty two plays, four rejected. Four warnings, one per bad row. One duplicate dropped. The chart written. When this pipeline runs unattended at night, this log is how anyone finds out what happened, and the warnings are the to-do list.

The last tool for trust is one we already have: the compiler. By default it is lenient, but it can be told to be strict, and project dot scala now does that, on its last line, with three options. Dash Werror turns every warning into an error, so the build fails instead of scrolling past a warning nobody reads. Dash Wunused colon all warns about anything unused: imports, values, parameters. And strictEquality changes what double equals means. Normally Scala lets you compare any two values with double equals, even values that can never be equal, like a TrackId and a UserId, and the answer is simply false, every time. With strict equality, two types can only be compared if a CanEqual given says they may. We turned these on over the existing code, and the table on the right lists what the compiler found, from two branches of the spine. Four comparisons of Json and Device values, inside pattern matches, which became legal once those enums derived CanEqual. And an unused import in Transform dot scala, ZoneOffset, left over since course six. Each finding was real, and each fix is in this section: the import is gone, the enums derive CanEqual, and TrackId and UserId each give themselves a CanEqual, but only with their own kind. The terminal shows the result. The whole project, tests included, compiles cleanly. And in the REPL, the mistake strict equality exists to catch: TrackId t zero one, double equals, UserId u zero one. Refused: values of types TrackId and UserId cannot be compared. playstream is now tested, logged and reviewed by its own compiler. In the next course, it meets ten million plays.

A real music service does not play forty songs a day. It plays millions. To see what happens to playstream at that scale, we need a day of that size, and we will make one ourselves. Gen dot scala is a generator. Look at line seven: at main def generate, with a parameter n of type Int. When a main method takes parameters, Scala parses them from the command line, so generate can be run with the number of plays to write. Line eight is the key to making it useful: a Random with a fixed seed. A seeded generator produces exactly the same sequence of numbers on every run, so every run of this course writes exactly the same ten million plays, and every result can be checked. Line sixteen plants a problem we will meet later in this course. Slow Tide has gone viral: forty percent of all plays are of that one track. The terminal runs it with dash M, which picks which main method to run: generate, ten million. About five hundred megabytes, and head shows its first lines, in the same format as the web player's export. Now, the code from course seven, which reads every line into a List and parses them all. It is in Scale dot scala, as a main method called naive. We run it with a limit of five hundred and twelve megabytes of heap, a realistic budget for a job sharing a machine. And it dies: OutOfMemoryError, Java heap space. Five hundred megabytes of text becomes far more than that once every line is a String object and every play a Play, all held at once. The diagram on the right shows where it failed. The next scene looks inside the JVM while it happens.

To see why the naive run died, we run it again with one more option, dash Xlog colon gc, which makes the JVM log every pause of its garbage collector. On the left is the code that was running: read every line into a List, then parse them all. The JVM's collector here is G1, and the table explains its idea in three lines. New objects are created in the young part of the heap. Most objects in most programs die young, so a pause copies the few that are still in use somewhere safe, and frees everything else at once, cheaply. Objects that keep surviving are moved to the old part, and kept. On the right is the log, as a plot. Each point is one pause. The dots show how much of the heap was in use before the pause, and the line how much was still in use after it. In a healthy program, the line drops far below the dots at every pause, because most objects were garbage. Here, the line follows the dots almost exactly. Pause after pause, the collector looked for garbage and found almost none, because every line and every play was still in the List, still reachable, still alive. So the heap kept growing, towards the limit of five hundred and twelve megabytes, the dashed line. The count at the bottom says how it ended: about thirty pauses, each one freeing nothing, and then the OutOfMemoryError. This is the lesson the collector teaches. It can free anything you are no longer using, automatically. It cannot free anything you are still holding on to. A program that keeps every record of a big file in memory will run out, whatever the collector does. The fix is not a bigger heap. It is to stop holding on.

The fix is the idea from the end of course six: an Iterator, which reads one line at a time and forgets it when it has been used. Stream dot scala, in the editor, counts plays per track that way. countTracks opens the file with Using, so it is always closed. getLines returns an Iterator over its lines. Each line is parsed, the counted plays are kept, and each becomes a tiny Map from its track to one. Then foldLeft combines them, one at a time, into a running total, using the Monoid operator from course eight. The diagram on the right shows what is in memory at any moment: one line, one play, and the running total, which is a Map of just eight tracks. Nothing else is kept. A line is read, used, and becomes garbage straight away, which is exactly the kind of garbage the young collector frees cheaply. The terminal runs it with the same limit of five hundred and twelve megabytes. It finishes in seconds and prints the top tracks: t zero three, Slow Tide, with almost four point seven five million counted plays, a long way ahead of every other track, as the generator intended. And the last line measures the heap in use at the end: well under a hundred megabytes. The plot compares the two programs. The naive one needed more than the whole budget and died. The streaming one used a small fraction of it, and it would use the same small fraction for a hundred million plays, or a billion. That is what constant memory means: the memory a program needs depends on its state, here eight counts, not on the size of its input.

Streaming works, but how fast is it, and where does the time go? Guessing is the classic mistake here. Programmers are famously bad at predicting which part of a program is slow, so the rule is: measure first. Timing dot scala adds a small tool for that. timed takes a label and a block of code, passed by name so that it is not run until timed runs it. It notes the time, runs the block, prints how many milliseconds it took, and returns the block's result, so it can wrap any expression without changing what it computes. measure runs four passes over the ten million lines, each one doing a little more than the last. Read: just read every line, and count them. Split: also split each line at its commas. Parse: also turn each into a Play. Aggregate: the whole streaming count from the last section. The plot on the right shows the four timings from this run, and the table works out what each stage adds on its own. Simply reading the file takes over a second. Splitting the lines roughly doubles that. Parsing and validating adds a little more, and aggregating adds the rest. Two things stand out. First, everything is in the same range: no single stage dominates, so there is no single easy fix. Second, this whole pipeline runs on one core of a machine that has several. The work for one line never depends on another line, apart from adding up the totals at the end. And adding up totals, thanks to the Monoid, can happen in any grouping. So the obvious next step is not to make one stage faster. It is to use every core.

To work on several cores at once, the data has to be split into parts that can be processed independently. For counting plays per track, the natural split is by track: if all the plays of one track are in the same part, each part's counts are complete for its tracks. Shuffle dot scala does that split, in one pass over the file. partitionOf, at line eight, takes a line and the number of parts. It splits off just enough of the line to find the track id, takes the id's hashCode, a number computed from the text, and uses floorMod to turn it into a part number from zero to parts minus one. The same track always gives the same hash, so it always goes to the same part. The diagram on the right shows the route. partition opens one writer per part, sends every line to the writer its track picks, and closes them all at the end, in a finally block, so they are closed even if something fails. This is what the big data frameworks call a shuffle: moving every record to the place where its key is processed. We have just written one in a dozen lines. We split into four parts, one per core of this machine, and wc dash l counts the lines in each. Look at the numbers, and at the plot. Three partitions have about one and a half million plays each. The fourth has five and a half million: more than half of all the plays. Its tracks include Slow Tide, the viral track, and every one of its plays had to go to the same partition. Remember this plot. In the next section, it decides how fast the parallel version can be.

Parallel dot scala counts the four partitions. Line eleven does it the plain way, one partition after another, on one core, and combines the four partial counts with combineAll. Lines twelve to fifteen do the same work on every core. Future dot traverse starts one Future per partition. A Future is a computation that runs in the background, on a pool of threads that Scala manages, sized to the number of cores. Each Future counts its own partition, independently of the others. Await dot result waits for all four, and then, exactly as before, combineAll joins the partial counts. The diagram on the right shows the shape: split, count in parallel, combine. Notice what is not here. There are no locks, and no shared mutable state. Each Future reads its own file and builds its own immutable Map. The only place the results meet is combineAll, after every Future has finished. This is why immutability and the Monoid mattered. The partial counts can be combined in any order, because combine is associative, and the property test from course nine checked exactly that. The last line checks it again, for real: same answer, true. The plot shows the timings. On one core, about four seconds. On every core, faster, but only a little under twice as fast, not four times. With four cores, why not four times? Look back at the partition sizes. Three of the Futures finished their million and a half plays quickly, and then waited. The fourth had five and a half million, and the whole job could not finish until it did. A parallel job is only as fast as its biggest part.

When one key holds a large share of the data, the partition that gets it is overloaded, while the others sit idle. This is called skew, and it is one of the most common performance problems in data engineering. Viral tracks, celebrity accounts, a default value that half the rows share: real data is skewed all the time. The standard cure is called salting, and it takes a few lines, added to Shuffle dot scala beside the plain partitioner. saltedPartitionOf looks at the track. If it is one of the hot keys, here Slow Tide, the partition is chosen by the play's event id instead, which spreads that track's plays evenly over every partition. Every other track keeps its own partition, as before. But wait: the counts for Slow Tide will now be spread over four partitions, so no single partition has its complete count. Does that break the answer? No, and this is the payoff of the Monoid. Each partition produces a partial count for Slow Tide, and combineAll adds the four partials together. Combining is associative, so the answer is the same however the plays were split. The terminal partitions again with t zero three salted, and wc shows the new sizes, which the plot draws over the old ones. Instead of one partition with five and a half million plays, three have about two point seven million and one has a little less. Then the parallel count runs again. Same answer, true, and the table shows the speedup: from less than two times, to more than three times on four cores. Nothing about the counting changed. Only the split did. Balancing the work across partitions mattered more than anything we could have done to make a single stage faster.

One computation from course six cannot simply be split by key and counted: sessions. To find a listener's sessions, the plays must be in order, by listener and then by time. And sorting ten million lines with sorted would need them all in memory at once, which is exactly what failed at the start of this course. The answer is an external sort, and Sort dot scala builds one in two phases, shown in the diagram on the right. Phase one, lines eighteen to twenty four. Read the file in groups of one million lines, which do fit in memory. Sort each group by its key, the listener and then the start time, and write it to disk as a run. Ten groups make ten sorted runs. Phase two merges them. Each run is already sorted, so the smallest line overall must be the first line of one of the runs. A priority queue holds the current first line of each of the ten runs, ordered by key. Lines thirty four to thirty seven are the whole merge: take the smallest from the queue, write it out, and refill the queue from the run it came from. Repeat until every run is empty. At any moment, the merge holds only ten lines in memory, one per run, however large the file. The terminal runs it under the same five hundred and twelve megabyte limit, and it completes: ten sorted runs, ten million lines merged. ls counts the runs, and head shows the start of the result: listener u zero zero zero zero zero, in time order. A sessions pass can now stream through this file one listener at a time, in constant memory. This course built, by hand, the core ideas of every big data framework: streaming, shuffles, parallel partial aggregation, skew, and external sorting.

So far, playstream has been a batch job: run it, it reads everything, it finishes. But the phones upload all day, and the charts should follow them as they arrive. That is streaming, and this course builds a small streaming job by hand. First, some tidying, because the project has grown. The experiments from course ten now live in a folder called scale, and the JSON parser and decoder in a folder called json. scala-cli compiles every folder, so nothing else had to change. The streaming code goes in a new folder, stream. Uploads will arrive in a folder called inbox, and Watch dot scala notices them. It uses the JDK's WatchService. Line eleven registers the inbox with it, asking to hear about every file created there. Then the program lists what is already in the folder, so that a file arriving in the moment before the watch began is not missed. The loop takes events from the watcher, which blocks until something happens, and reads each new file. In the terminal, one command starts the watcher for two files, and in the background, a few seconds later, delivers two uploads into the inbox. Each one is copied next to the inbox first, then moved in with mv, so the file appears all at once, never half written, the same idea as the atomic writes of course seven. The diagram on the right follows one arrival. The watcher says it is watching for two more, then picked up b one, four events, and b two, three events, as they landed. That is the shape of every streaming system: wait for new data, process it, wait again. Next, a closer look at what is in those files.

Every play in a stream has two times, and confusing them is the root of most streaming bugs. Event time is when the play actually happened: started at. Arrival time is when the pipeline heard about it: here, uploaded at, a field every phone upload carries. Arrival dot scala keeps the two together. An Arrival is a Play and its upload time, and the extension method lateBy measures the gap between them, as a java dot time Duration. The terminal lists every play in the four test uploads with both clocks, and the plot on the right shows the gaps. Most plays were heard within the hour, because phones upload in batches, every so often. But two are very different, and the table at the bottom picks them out. e two zero one zero was played at twenty past eight in the evening and only heard about at twenty past eleven: almost three hours late. Its phone was out of signal. And e two zero one one was played at half past nine on the second of October and heard about at eight in the morning on the fourth: thirty four hours late. That phone was switched off for a day and a half. Both are real plays, and both must eventually count. The question this course answers is: when can the pipeline say that an hour's chart is final, if a play from that hour might still turn up a day later? Waiting forever is not an option, and neither is ignoring late plays. The answer will need both clocks: event time to decide which hour a play belongs to, and the progress of event time to decide when to stop waiting.

A streaming chart is not one total for all time. It is counts per period, and the simplest period is a tumbling window: fixed, back to back, never overlapping. Here, one window per hour. Windows dot scala defines them. windowOf, highlighted, takes a play's start time and cuts it to the hour. A play that started at ten past eight, or five to nine, belongs to the eight o'clock window, as the table on the right shows. windowEnd says when a window's hour is over. And countWindows counts plays per track in each window. Look at how little it takes: each play becomes a Map from its window to a Map from its track to one, and combineAll merges them all. The nested Map works because course eight's given builds a Monoid for a Map whenever its values have one, and a Map of counts does. The terminal runs it over the first three uploads, all at once, and the diagram shows the four windows of the second of October. Eight o'clock: Slow Tide two, Night Bus two. Nine o'clock: one each of three tracks. Ten and eleven o'clock, a few more. Notice that this is event time at work: e two zero one zero, the play that arrived three hours late, was put in the eight o'clock window, where it happened, not in the window when it arrived. But this run cheated a little. It read all three uploads before counting, so it already knew about the late play. A real stream has to publish the eight o'clock chart at some point, without knowing what is still on its way. Deciding when, is the job of a watermark.

A watermark is the stream's estimate of how far event time has surely got. Ours is simple, and line four of Watermark dot scala sets it up: an allowed lateness of one hour. The watermark is the latest event time seen so far, minus that hour. The rule, in the diagram on the right, is that once the watermark passes the end of a window, the window is final. Its counts are published and never reopened. A play that arrives later for a final window does not change it. It goes to a late report instead, so it is never silently lost. This version is written the way you might first write it: a loop over the four uploads, with three vars for the latest time, the open windows and the closed ones. Read the terminal batch by batch, with the table beside it. After b one, the latest play is at two minutes past nine, so the watermark is at two minutes past eight, and no window can be final yet. After b two, the watermark reaches five past nine, past the end of the eight o'clock window, so eight o'clock becomes final: Slow Tide two, Night Bus one. After b three, nine o'clock is final, and e two zero one zero, the three hour late play, arrives for eight o'clock, which is already closed. It goes to the late report. After b four, the watermark jumps to the fourth of October, closing ten and eleven o'clock, and the thirty four hour late play is reported late too. Notice the trade-off in that one hour. A longer allowed lateness catches more late plays, but publishes every chart later. Every streaming system makes exactly this choice.

The loop in the last section works, but its state is spread across three vars, changed in place in the middle of the loop. That makes it hard to save, hard to test, and impossible to restart. Job dot scala rewrites it the way course six taught: as a fold. All the state becomes one immutable value, a case class called StreamState: the latest event time, the open windows, and the windows already closed. step, the heart of it, is a pure function. It takes the state and one batch of plays, and returns two things: the next state, and an Output saying which windows became final and which plays were late. It reads nothing and writes nothing, so it can be tested with plain values. The diagram on the right shows the shape. Then the whole stream is one line: batches, foldLeft, starting from the empty state, calling step for each batch. Each step's output is printed, and the next state is passed on. The terminal and the table show the result, batch by batch: one final window after b two, one final and one late after b three, two final and one late after b four, and one window still open at the end, for the fourth of October. Exactly the same answers as the loop with vars. That is the point: nothing about the logic changed, only its shape. And the shape matters for what comes next. Because the whole of the stream's memory is now one value, it can be written to disk after every batch, and read back after a crash. That is what the next section does.

A real stream runs for weeks, and anything that runs for weeks will crash. When it starts again, it must know where it was. Checkpoint dot scala saves that. checkpointJson turns the state, and the list of files already done, into a Json value, using our own Json type from course seven, and loadCheckpoint reads it back with our own parser. tick is the job itself: load the checkpoint, find the files in the inbox that are not done yet, fold over them with step, write each batch's outputs, then save the new checkpoint. Final windows go to one file per hour, and late plays are appended to out, late dot csv. And there is one more line, highlighted: if the environment variable CRASH is set, the program stops dead with exit code one hundred thirty seven, after writing its outputs but before saving the checkpoint. That simulates the worst moment to crash. Now follow the terminal. Two uploads are delivered and tick processes them, then saves a checkpoint: two files done. b three arrives, and the next tick processes it, writes its outputs, and crashes, exit one hundred thirty seven. The checkpoint still says two files done. So the next tick, the restart, processes b three again, from the beginning, and this time saves the checkpoint. Nothing was lost. But look at the last command, and the table on the right. The late report contains e two zero one zero twice. The first run appended it, crashed, and the second run appended it again. The windows were fine, because each was rewritten whole. Processing a batch at least once is easy. Exactly once needs one more idea.

A replayed batch must leave the outputs exactly as if it had run once. There are two ways things get counted twice, and this section closes both. The first is the one we just saw: an output that a replay appends to. The fix, in Checkpoint dot scala, is to write each batch's late plays to a file named after the batch, with the atomic write from course seven, so that a replay replaces the file instead of adding to it. The second is a duplicate in the data itself: a phone that did not get a reply and uploads the same plays again, in a new file. The fix is in step, highlighted in Job dot scala. The state now remembers every event id it has counted, in seen. fresh keeps only the plays not seen before, and the rest are counted as repeats. seen is saved in the checkpoint with everything else. The diagram on the right shows the two rules. The terminal replays the scene from the last section, starting after the first two batches. b three arrives, the job crashes before its checkpoint, and the restart processes b three again: the same final window, the same late play. Then a phone re-uploads b two, under a new name. tick reads it: zero final, zero late, three already counted. And the late report, at the bottom, holds e two zero one zero exactly once. A crash at the worst moment, and a duplicate upload, and the outputs are exactly what one clean run would have produced. This is what streaming frameworks mean by exactly once: not that nothing is ever processed twice, but that processing twice changes nothing. playstream can now follow its uploads live. One course to go: shipping it.

A program that will run on other machines cannot have its folders and limits written into the code. They have to be settings, and settings come from several places. Config dot scala collects them in four layers, shown on the right. Defaults, written in the code, so the program always works. A file, playstream dot conf, for the settings of one installation. The environment, for settings a scheduler or a container passes in, each starting with PLAYSTREAM underscore. And flags on the command line, for one run. Each layer overrides the one before, so a flag always has the last word. Look at how each layer is read, because each uses a Scala pattern you have not seen yet: a string pattern. In fromFile, case s, dollar key, equals, dollar value, matches a line with an equals sign in it, and pulls out the parts on either side. In fromEnv, case s PLAYSTREAM underscore dollar key matches only variables with that prefix, and takes what follows. In fromFlags, case s dash dash key equals value matches a flag. The same s that builds strings can take them apart. layered then lists every setting with the layer it came from: the layers are flattened in order, and toMap keeps the last value for each key. The terminal shows it. playstream dot conf sets top to ten and out to reports. With no other layers, data and zone come from the defaults, and out and top from the file. Then a second run, with PLAYSTREAM underscore TOP set to three and a zone flag. Now top comes from the environment and the zone from the flag. The table at the bottom shows that second run.

Course ten left playstream with many entry points, generate, partition, tick and more, each picked with scala-cli's dash M. A shipped program needs one front door. Main dot scala now has it: at main def playstream, which takes all its arguments. It loads the settings first, from all four layers. Then it removes the flags from the arguments, and matches what is left against the jobs it knows. chart computes the daily charts. stream runs one tick of the streaming job from course eleven. Anything else prints a usage line, so a typo gets help instead of a stack trace. The diagram on the right shows the routing. chart itself is the batch pipeline from the earlier courses, now driven by the settings. It reads every export from the configured data folder, keeps the counted plays, groups them by day in the configured time zone, and writes the configured number of top tracks into one partition per day, under the configured output folder. In the terminal, playstream chart, with a flag asking for the top three. The log tells the story: two files read, the same four rejected lines with their reasons, one duplicate dropped, and a chart written for each day. Notice where the charts went: into a folder called reports, not out, because playstream dot conf, from the last section, says so, while the flag changed only the number of rows. cat shows the first of October's chart, and the table on the right repeats it. And playstream help, a job it does not know, prints the usage line. This is the shape of almost every command line tool: one name, a few verbs, and options that adjust them.

Until now, running playstream meant having scala-cli and its source code. To ship it, it becomes one file. scala-cli's package command, with dash dash assembly, compiles everything and writes a single jar: our compiled classes, and the Scala library they need, all together, as the diagram on the right shows. dash dash main-class says which entry point to start: playstream. The terminal shows it writing playstream dot jar, about ten megabytes, and even tells us how to run it: dot slash playstream dot jar. The jar starts with a few lines of shell script, so on Linux and macOS it can be run directly, and Java finds the rest. Anyone with Java can now run the pipeline, with no Scala installation and no source code. And it works: playstream dot jar chart, top three, writes the two daily charts, and tail shows the last two lines of its log. But building the jar revealed something, and it is why Log dot scala is open in the editor. Until now, the format of the log lines came from a javaProp line in project dot scala. That file is read by scala-cli, and a jar knows nothing about it, so the first packaged run logged in Java's default format, with dates and class names on separate lines. The fix moves the setting into the code itself: before the logger is created, line six sets the format as a system property. The javaProp line is gone from project dot scala. The table at the bottom lists what does not travel with the jar: the tests, which are test only, and project dot scala's settings. That is a good question to ask before shipping anything: what does my program depend on that is not inside it?

The last job is to make the charts available to other programs, over HTTP. The JDK includes a small HTTP server, and Server dot scala uses it in about twenty lines. serve, at the bottom, creates a server on port eight thousand and eighty, and gives it one handler, for every path starting with slash charts slash. The handler takes the date from the path, asks answer what to send, logs the request, and writes the response: a status code, a content type of application slash json, and the body. answer, highlighted, is where the care goes. It builds the path of that day's chart file, but only uses it if the date really is a date, four digits, two and two, and the file exists. Anything else, including a path that tries to climb out of the folder, like dot dot slash, gets a four oh four, before any file is touched. chartJson reads the chart's CSV with readCsvLine, the quoting-aware reader from course nine, and turns each row into a Json object, with our own Json type, rendered as text. The diagram on the right follows one request. The terminal runs the jar in the background with the serve job, waits for it to start, and asks curl for two charts. The first of October answers with status two hundred and a JSON array: Slow Tide, Mara Quell, six plays, then Night Bus and Northern Lights. Christmas Day answers four oh four, with an error message in JSON. The server's log line for each request comes first, because the handler logs before it replies. Then kill stops the server. playstream now ingests, validates, aggregates, streams, and serves.

This is the map from the first course, and now every part of it is lit. On the left, what comes in: the web player's daily exports, the phones' uploads, which can arrive days late, and the catalog. In the middle, playstream itself, and every box is something you built. The model, from course five: plays and events as types, ids that cannot be mixed up, a Play that cannot be invalid. Parsing, from courses four and seven: CSV with every bad row reported, and a JSON parser written by hand. The transformations from course six: charts, sessions and deduplication. One Monoid and one derived codec, from course eight, behind every aggregation and every report. The scale work from course ten: ten million plays in constant memory, a shuffle, every core, skew handled, and a sort larger than memory. And the stream from course eleven: event time, windows, watermarks, checkpoints, and exactly once. Underneath, the tests and the strict compiler from course nine, and the jar from this course. On the right is the result, the real output of the packaged program: the first of October's chart, served as JSON, and a clear answer for a day with no chart. Two things are worth noticing about all of it. First, every line ran: every output in this course was produced by the code on screen, and checked again before it was shown. Second, it uses nothing but Scala's standard library and the JDK. Every idea that the big data frameworks are built on, you have now built by hand, at a size you can read in an afternoon. The last section shows where each of them leads.

Every part of playstream has an industrial-strength counterpart, and you now know what each one is doing underneath. The scale folder becomes Apache Spark. Spark runs the same ideas, partitions, shuffles, partial aggregation, salting and external sorts, across a cluster of machines instead of the cores of one, and its main API is written in Scala, so the code looks like what you wrote in course six. The stream folder becomes Apache Flink, or Spark's own streaming: event time, windows, watermarks and exactly-once checkpoints are their core concepts, with the same names. The inbox becomes Apache Kafka: a durable log of events that many consumers can read and replay, which is what a folder of upload files was standing in for. The Futures of course ten become Cats Effect or ZIO, libraries that treat concurrency and resources as values, in the same spirit as Either and Option. The JDK's HTTP server becomes http4s or Tapir, with routes and JSON codecs derived from types, like the CSV codec of course eight. And scala-cli, which was enough for one project, becomes sbt or Mill when a project grows into many modules and published libraries. None of these will feel like magic now. When Spark talks about a shuffle, you have written one. When Flink talks about a watermark, you have decided when an hour is final. When a library asks you for an implicit Ordering or derives a codec, you know what the compiler is doing. That was the point of building playstream by hand. Thank you for watching, and happy building.
